articles.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction after service in Ukraine is restored
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operatio...
articles.body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.

Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.

Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks .

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

Musk admits he was behind Starlink's speed restriction

After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defenses since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky , a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

Restriction led to tensions between Ukraine and the US

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."

Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.

Russia and Ukraine have continued to target each other

Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday.

Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.

Ukraine's General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.

Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.

Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said drones "reached a northern industrial hub."

Online retailer Ozon said Saturday that its logistics center in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

articles.title: The last two countries with polio: Why Pakistan and Afghanistan are struggling to eliminate it
articles.summary: As countries mark World Polio Day, the disease remains entrenched in Pakistan and Afghanistan, even as it has been eliminated from almost every other part
articles.body: As countries mark World Polio Day, the disease remains entrenched in Pakistan and Afghanistan, even as it has been eliminated from almost every other part of the world. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) is marking the day with a plain message: political commitment matters more than ever.Afghanistan has emerged as the bigger concern this year, reporting 42 cases of wild poliovirus type 1 in 2026, twice the 21 recorded in the whole of 2025. Pakistan, meanwhile, has reported six cases, down sharply from 31 last year. The two countries have together reported 48 cases so far this year, against 52 in all of 2025.The resurgence follows a dramatic reversal in progress.In 2023, the two countries reported just 12 cases between them, with six each. The total surged to 99 in 2024, highlighting how fragile the gains against the virus remain.The threat extends beyond reported cases of paralysis. Wild poliovirus continues to be detected in environmental samples, indicating that the virus is circulating even in places where no paralytic cases have been identified.Why is polio surviving today?Polio is a highly infectious viral disease that mainly affects children under five.It spreads primarily through the faecal-oral route, often in settings where sanitation and hygiene are inadequate.Most infections produce no obvious symptoms. In a small proportion of cases, however, the virus attacks the nervous system and causes irreversible paralysis. There is no cure for polio-induced paralysis, making vaccination the principal means of prevention.Eradication requires every child to be reached, including those who miss routine immunisation or vaccination campaigns. In Pakistan and Afghanistan, insecurity, restricted access, mistrust and population movement have left gaps that allow the virus to keep circulating.Dr Sunil Sareen, a paediatrician at Apollo Spectra Hospital in Delhi, told TOI that political instability and uneven vaccination coverage had made it harder to reach children in high-risk areas. “Even a few unvaccinated children can help spread the disease,” he said.The consequences of failure would extend far beyond the region.WHO has warned that if eradication efforts collapse, polio could cause as many as 200,000 new cases annually worldwide within a decade.The virus has already demonstrated its ability to travel: in October 2025, wild poliovirus was detected in a routine sewage sample in Hamburg, Germany.A chase that is almost 40 years oldThe global eradication effort began in 1988, when the World Health Assembly adopted a resolution to eliminate polio worldwide. The resulting Global Polio Eradication Initiative brought together governments, the World Health Organisation (WHO), UNICEF, Rotary International and other partners to coordinate vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response.The progress has been extraordinary. According to the WHO, the number of wild poliovirus cases has fallen by more than 99% since 1988, when an estimated 350,000 cases occurred annually across more than 125 endemic countries. Wild poliovirus types 2 and 3 have been declared eradicated. Type 1 is the only wild strain that continues to circulate.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(message,function(e){if(e.data[datawrapper-height]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(iframe);for(var n in e.data[datawrapper-height])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[datawrapper-height][n]+px;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();But eradication is different from simply reducing cases. A country can go years without reporting a paralytic infection and still have undetected transmission. To eradicate the virus globally, transmission must be interrupted everywhere, including in communities that are difficult to reach or where vaccination coverage remains uneven.Hence, the finish line keeps moving. The original goal was the year 2000. The GPEI now aims to certify wild poliovirus eradication by the end of 2027.In the past decade alone, more than $3 billion has been spent on the effort in Afghanistan and Pakistan.India beat it in the hardest placeIndia’s own story shows that this can be done. When the Pulse Polio programme began in 1995, the country was recording an estimated 50,000 to 150,000 cases a year. As late as 2009, it still accounted for about 60% of the world’s cases.The risks were greatest in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Together they held about 300 million people, with roughly 5,00,000 births a month and heavy migration in and out. The CDC says that if polio could be ended there, it could be ended in the toughest settings anywhere.The method was relentless. India added house-to-house vaccination to find children who were not brought to fixed sites. During national immunisation days since 2000, more than 2.3 million vaccinators visited about 209 million households to reach over 170 million children under five. Transit teams at bus stops, railway stations and on trains vaccinated nearly 10 million children in each campaign.Trust mattered as much as logistics. Teams included at least one woman and one member of the local community, to ease entry into homes. Religious and community leaders were brought in where families were reluctant. Vaccinated children’s fingers were marked, and visited houses were marked too. Every home was numbered in detailed microplans, and independent checks measured coverage after each round.Sareen said Pakistan and Afghanistan could learn from India's combination of door-to-door vaccination and community engagement. Local healthcare professionals, religious figures and community leaders can help counter misinformation, while follow-ups and outreach to migrant populations can help reach children who miss doses.Science also helped. India switched to more effective vaccines, monovalent in 2005 and bivalent in 2010. The last case of wild polio was reported in Howrah, West Bengal, on January 13, 2011. On March 27, 2014, WHO declared the whole 11-country South-East Asia Region polio-free.India has not stopped. It still holds one national and two sub-national immunisation days every year, and has added the injectable polio vaccine to routine immunisation.Many of the tools that worked in India are exactly the ones now restricted or threatened across the border.Afghanistan: No knocking on doorsAfghanistan’s surge traces back to how vaccines are delivered. The Taliban authorities restricted house-to-house vaccination in September 2024, after briefly allowing it across most of the country earlier that year. WHO says none has been held since October 2024. Campaigns now rely largely on mosques and other fixed sites.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(message,function(e){if(e.data[datawrapper-height]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(iframe);for(var n in e.data[datawrapper-height])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[datawrapper-height][n]+px;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();It had been working. In June 2024, house-to-house vaccination reached 95% of target children, the first use of the method in the South Region in more than five years, though Kandahar stayed on the site-based model.Now the WHO committee says site-based campaigns “often fail to reach all children, particularly younger children.” It also flags the limited role of women health workers, the very people India put on every team. The worst-hit area is the south, where the committee says intense transmission continues. This week’s six new cases came from Kandahar, Nangarhar and Kabul.Kamal Shah, a former Unicef communications officer, was quoted by VOA as saying that a main problem is “shortcomings in vaccination campaigns.”Pakistan: Bullets, rumours and refusalsPakistan has no ban on door-to-door vaccination. Its problem is safety. On May 18, the first day of a campaign to vaccinate more than 19 million children across 79 high-risk districts, gunmen killed two police officers guarding vaccination teams in Bajaur.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(message,function(e){if(e.data[datawrapper-height]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(iframe);for(var n in e.data[datawrapper-height])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[datawrapper-height][n]+px;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();In April, a policeman was killed in Balochistan and another was injured in Hangu. Officials say more than 200 polio workers and police escorts have died since the 1990s.Militants often claim the drives are a foreign plot to sterilise children, and rumours in rural areas include a claim that the vaccine is a CIA plot. Nature adds that some families refuse vaccines or question them when needs like clean water and sanitation go unmet.The WHO committee welcomed Pakistan’s strong political support and generally high reported coverage. But campaign quality varies by district, especially in southern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Transmission also persists in Karachi.Pakistan’s progress is real. Cases are down 99.8% from an estimated 20,000 a year in the early 1990s. On a visit this year, WHO regional director Hanan Balkhy said Pakistan “has a genuine opportunity to interrupt poliovirus transmission.”What the sewers showParalytic cases reveal only part of the outbreak. Poliovirus can circulate in the intestine without causing obvious symptoms, allowing infected people to spread it before a case is identified.Health authorities therefore test sewage and other environmental samples for the virus. A positive sample can reveal transmission even when no nearby paralytic case has been reported.By mid-August, 176 sewage samples across the two countries had tested positive for wild poliovirus this year: 118 in Pakistan and 58 in Afghanistan.Pakistan had reported only three cases at that point. In 2025, the two countries recorded 745 positive samples.The WHO committee said transmission persisted through even the latest low season, from October 2025 to April 2026, and that it continues in both countries.One virus, one borderThe remaining outbreak follows a geography that crosses national boundaries. Pakistan and Afghanistan share a long border, and the movement of people between them creates opportunities for the virus to travel between communities.In its August assessment, the WHO emergency committee identified three critical areas of continued transmission: southern Afghanistan, southern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan, and Karachi.It also highlighted two cross-border corridors: southern Afghanistan and Pakistan's Quetta region, and north-western Pakistan and south-eastern Afghanistan.The hotspots and corridors show how transmission links communities across the border, particularly where children have missed vaccination.Population movements have added to the challenge. In 2024, the committee recorded more than 600,000 returnees from Pakistan to Afghanistan, with estimates suggesting that up to 1.7 million people were affected. It also found evidence that some poliovirus strains detected in Afghanistan had been brought back by returnees.The movement remains a concern. Xinhua has reported that Afghan health authorities attributed the recent rise in cases partly to the mass return of Afghan refugees from Pakistan.Mobile and displaced families can be missed by routine and supplementary campaigns, making coordinated vaccination and surveillance essential.Sareen warned that continued transmission also posed a risk to neighbouring countries, including India. Although India was declared polio-free in 2014, he said it must maintain high immunisation coverage to reduce the risk of reintroduction through international travel.The money is shrinkingFunding is tightening at the worst moment. The GPEI cut its 2026 operating budget by 30%. For 2027, its oversight board approved about $778 million, roughly $65 million less.Surveillance funding stays at the reduced level, and the programme admits the cuts have affected “the speed and scale” of eradication in some places.Nature ties part of the squeeze to the US exit from WHO in January, which ended American funding for WHO’s polio work, and to the earlier dismantling of USAID, which disrupted $85 million for surveillance and health communication.Sareen warned that funding cuts could weaken vaccination and surveillance. He called for sustained financing, coordinated campaigns, better monitoring of mobile populations and greater involvement of community leaders and female health workers.Others are stepping in: Rotary members raise about $50 million a year, Saudi Arabia pledged $500 million, Pakistan $154 million and the Gates Foundation $1.2 billion for 2026 to 2029.There is also fatigue. One source cited by science journal Nature said that “politicians focus on real problems, not on something that is basically gone.”What nextPolio has not left the rest of the world either. GPEI’s latest update lists vaccine-derived cases in countries including DR Congo, Nigeria, South Sudan and Chad.These come from a weakened virus in the oral vaccine that can spread where immunisation is low. That is why the goal is finishing the job, not just holding the line.The committee has urged Afghanistan to restore house-to-house vaccination wherever possible and Pakistan to protect vaccination workers and improve campaign quality in weaker districts. GPEI is also reviewing its eradication timeline after assessing progress in 2026.Sareen said the two countries must prioritise children who have missed routine immunisation and ensure that vaccination, surveillance and cross-border coordination remain adequately funded.India’s lesson is not that polio is easy to beat. It is that it can be beaten with doors opened, women on every team, communities on board and money that does not run out. The last two countries now have the vaccine. What they lack is steady access, safety for vaccinators and the funds to keep going.The world has already shown that polio can be pushed to the brink of eradication. The final test is whether Pakistan and Afghanistan can reach the children who have been missed repeatedly and keep reaching them until the virus has nowhere left to circulate.

articles.title: Starlink seems to be working normally again in Ukraine
articles.summary: Elon Musk reportedly ordered SpaceX to throttle Ukraine's Starlink access.
articles.body:
SpaceX appears to have lifted restrictions the Ukrainian military’s of use Starshield — the military-grade version of the company’s Starlink internet system.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara told reporters that Starshield appears to be working normally again, although the military is still conducting tests and has not received an explanation for the restrictions.

This follows a 10-day period where Ukrainian drones would lose internet connectivity when flying at speeds of around 100 miles per hour, resulting in the military losing control of some drones, while others became more vulnerable because they were flying more slowly.

President Donald Trump reportedly called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Wednesday and asked him to restore Starshield service. Both Trump and Musk have criticized Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, with Musk recently posting , “Zelensky has gone too far.”

The WSJ previously reported that Musk ordered SpaceX to throttle Ukraine’s Starlink access, though some sources claimed he’d discussed it with the Trump administration first. Musk claimed in a post on X that Ukraine had “violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”

“Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately,” Musk said. “This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact.”

articles.title: Researchers removed invasive reeds at a Connecticut pond, reducing their growth by 98% and increasing native plant diversity by 39% over six years
articles.summary: Connecticut’s Highstead Pond recorded a 39% increase in native plant species richness after researchers began removing an invasive reed.
articles.body: Connecticut’s Highstead Pond recorded a 39% increase in native plant species richness after researchers began removing an invasive reed. Over six years, researchers monitored vegetation at Highstead Preserve, where the reed Phragmites australis had covered 30% of the pond’s shoreline. According to the study published in BioOne Complete, titled ‘Response of a Wetland Plant Community to Management of Phragmites Australis (Poaceae) in Southwestern Connecticut ‘, repeated herbicide treatments achieved 98% mortality of the invasive grass, while native plant richness increased by approximately four species per plot on average by 2017. However, non-native plant richness also rose during the study, highlighting the challenges of restoring wetland vegetation through invasive species management.How did invasive Phragmites spread at Highstead PondBefore the management programme began, Phragmites australis covered 30% of the shoreline around Highstead Pond. The reed formed several small, dense patches measuring less than 100 square metres and one larger patch of approximately 1,300 square metres. The species is a perennial grass native to Eurasia that is now found across temperate regions of North America, including freshwater, brackish and salt marsh environments.According to the researchers, relatively little information was available about the effectiveness of different management strategies and the responses of plant communities following the removal of Phragmites australis. To assess the impact of treatment, they monitored vegetation around the pond over six years, comparing plant densities and species richness before and after the reed was treated. In 2012, before herbicide application, the team randomly placed 28 one-square-metre plots in areas invaded by the reed. They counted live stems of vascular plant species, with a separate method used to estimate the abundance of grasses and other plants growing in overlapping clumps.How did researchers compare three methods of reed removalThe team used three techniques to apply a glyphosate-based herbicide: hand wiping, a long-handled brush applicator and spraying with a backpack sprayer. The hand-wipe method involved wiping the leaves and upper half of each stem, while the wand method used a long-handled brush to treat the same parts of the plant. The spray method applied the herbicide to the whole plant.The first year of treatment produced different results across the three methods. The researchers reported a 72% reduction in Phragmites australis using the handwipe approach, compared with reductions of 20% to 32% for the wand and spray treatments. The spray method also caused greater damage to other herbaceous vegetation. Stem densities of non-Phragmites herbs declined by 76% in the spray treatment, while they remained largely unchanged in the handwipe and wand treatments. Herb species richness in the spray-treated plots fell by 50%, from an average of 12.6 species per plot to 6.3. Following these results, the researchers used the handwipe method to treat all remaining reed stems in subsequent years.How did native plants recover after invasive reed removalBy 2014, following the second year of treatment, the density of Phragmites australis stems had declined by 98% across the 28 plots compared with the 2012 levels. The researchers also recorded increases in other herbaceous plants. Herb densities increased by 207% across all plots, while the original spray-treated plots recorded a 390% increase. In those spray-treated plots, herb species richness recovered from an average of 6.3 species in 2013 to 12.3 species in 2014.The study found that the recovery continued through 2017. Across all plots, herb species richness exceeded the pre-treatment level by almost four species per plot on average, representing a 29% increase. Woody stem density and woody species richness also increased between 2014 and 2017, by 128% and 103%, respectively. By 2017, ten species occurred in at least 40% of the sampled plots, compared with seven species meeting that frequency threshold before treatment. The researchers said this indicated a more even distribution of plant species than in 2013 or before the management programme began.How did native plant diversity increase by 39% after invasive reed removalThe study’s findings showed that native plant species richness increased by approximately four species per plot on average in 2017 compared with the pre-treatment measurements taken in 2012. This represented a 39% increase in native species richness across the plots. Non-native species richness also increased during the same period, rising by an average of 0.75 species per plot, or 110%.The researchers also recorded an increase in Microstegium vimineum, another invasive grass. It occurred in 18% of the plots during the first year after treatment and in 54% of the plots by 2017. The study therefore documented increases in both native and non-native plant diversity following the removal of Phragmites australis. The authors noted that removing one dominant non-native species can lead to greater species richness among both native and non-native plants in areas where other non-native species are already prevalent.The researchers concluded that hand wiping was the most effective method for managing Phragmites australis in relatively small areas, although it was more time-consuming than spraying. They also highlighted the ability of the wetland plant community to recover after the initial damage caused by the spray treatment. However, the study found that the invasive reed could regenerate after herbicide treatment. The authors reported achieving 98% mortality only after multiple years of treatment and said continued spot treatment of new stems would likely be needed each year into the foreseeable future.The findings, published by the New England Botanical Club in Rhodora, provide a six-year record of changes in vegetation following invasive reed management at Highstead Pond. The results documented a 98% reduction in reed stem density by 2014, a 39% increase in native plant species richness by 2017 and a simultaneous increase in non-native species richness during the study period.

articles.title: For 155 years, scientists believed a solar storm delayed a train in Exeter, England, in 1841, but the railway did not exist until 1846; researchers now say the storm and the 16-minute delay really happened in 1848
articles.summary: For more than 150 years, a reported 16-minute train delay in Exeter, England, was cited as a possible early example of a solar storm disrupting human
articles.body: For more than 150 years, a reported 16-minute train delay in Exeter, England, was cited as a possible early example of a solar storm disrupting human technology. But a railway timetable revealed a problem with the story: the railway line in question did not exist in 1841. According to a report published by ScienceDaily on October 21, 2026, researchers have now traced the incident to October 18, 1848, using historical railway records, newspaper accounts and measurements of Earth’s magnetic field. The findings were published in the journal Space Weather.The train delay that could not have happened in 1841The mystery originated in an account published anonymously in the scientific journal Nature on October 5, 1871. It described a “very intense magnetic disturbance” on October 18, 1841, which allegedly interfered with railway telegraph equipment in Exeter, a city in southwest England. According to the account, the disturbance prevented railway staff from establishing whether the track ahead, near the village of Starcross, was clear. As a result, the scheduled 10.05 pm express train from Exeter towards Newton Abbot was held up for 16 minutes.The report also described how the railway superintendent initially suspected that someone was tampering with the instruments because they would not function properly. The incident later attracted scientific interest because it appeared to document solar activity interfering with electrical infrastructure decades before modern power grids and satellite networks existed.However, the timeline did not withstand closer scrutiny. Researchers found that the railway section connecting Exeter with Starcross opened only on May 30, 1846, almost five years after the supposed incident. The line reached Newton Abbot later that year.The discrepancy prompted scientists to investigate whether the original report contained an incorrect date. The British Geological Survey (BGS), which participated in the international research effort, said the team compared railway timetables, historical newspapers, solar observations, aurora reports and digitised geomagnetic records.Why researchers believe the incident happened in 1848The evidence pointed to October 18, 1848, rather than October 18, 1841. Researchers examining historical railway timetables found that a 10.05 pm departure from Exeter towards Starcross was scheduled during a period spanning March 1848 to July 1849. That made October 1848 a plausible date for the reported delay.More importantly, historical magnetic measurements showed strong geomagnetic activity on October 18, 1848. Records preserved in the Greenwich Observatory archive documented significant changes in Earth’s magnetic field around the time of the alleged incident. Reports of sunspots and auroras observed across Britain and Europe offered additional evidence of heightened solar activity.The researchers concluded that the combination of railway records and magnetic observations strongly supported the revised date. The original account, published three decades after the event, appears to have contained a typographical error.The study, titled 'Did Space Weather Delay the 10:05 p.m. Train Departure From Exeter on 18 October 1841?', was led by James A. Wild of Lancaster University. Its international team included researchers from the British Geological Survey, RMIT University, Natural Resources Canada, Baylor University and RAL Space in the UK.The researchers could not recover the original source material behind the 1871 account, so the precise circumstances cannot be established with absolute certainty. Their conclusion is that the train delay most likely occurred in 1848, not that every detail of the original story has been independently confirmed.What is a solar storm, and how can it affect a railway?Space weather refers to changes in the environment around Earth caused by solar activity. The Sun can produce eruptions that send charged particles and magnetic fields into space. When these disturbances interact with Earth’s magnetic environment, they can trigger geomagnetic storms.Such storms can generate unwanted electrical currents in long conductors, including wires used by telegraph networks. In the 1840s, railways were beginning to rely on electric telegraphs to communicate between signal stations and establish whether sections of track were occupied or clear.These systems helped railway workers coordinate train movements across distances. articles.title: New Zealand began removing invasive weeds from Staveley Camp forest in 2017; years of monitoring later found native regeneration and growing birdlife
articles.summary: A patch of native forest can take years to show what careful restoration has achieved.
articles.body: A patch of native forest can take years to show what careful restoration has achieved. At Staveley Camp in mid-Canterbury, New Zealand, the work began in 2017 with a modest effort to control invasive plants that were spreading through an existing forest remnant, as reported by Environment Canterbury Regional Council. Since then, the project has involved sustained weed removal, pest control and help from local volunteers, schools and environmental groups. Monitoring carried out over five years has since recorded more native plants growing back in cleared areas and changes in the birds using the forest. The results have drawn attention to the value of protecting surviving native habitat, rather than relying solely on creating new areas of woodland.Staveley Camp native forest restoration helps invasive weed removal revive native plantsWhen Gen de Spa began working at Staveley Camp in 2017, her initial contract covered 150 hours of controlling cotoneaster and Darwin’s barberry, two invasive plants that had become established in the forest. It soon became apparent that the work would require a much longer commitment. Seed-producing trees and shrubs were spreading through the area, making it harder for native vegetation to recover.Over the following years, the restoration team removed hundreds of invasive sycamores, rowans, hawthorns, elderberries and cherry trees. Environment Canterbury, the regional council responsible for the project’s funding since 2017, supported the work as part of efforts to protect existing native forest.The results have varied across the site, but areas receiving sustained weed control have begun to regenerate naturally. De Spa, who has served as forest care coordinator for nine years, reported that native plants were returning in a range of forms and at a faster pace than she had expected in some places. A particularly welcome discovery was a mahoe plant, a native New Zealand tree that she had not previously encountered at the site. Birds may have carried its seeds into the forest.Staveley Camp restoration brings more kererū, fantails and silvereyesThe return of native vegetation has coincided with changes in the birds seen at Staveley Camp. Kererū, New Zealand’s native wood pigeon, are now regularly observed in flocks, alongside pīwakawaka, or fantails, and tauhou, also known as silvereyes. De Spa recalled, “For the first six years I watched the kererū population sit at two or three birds,” Gen said. “Then in 2024 it jumped to four and in 2025 to seven.”Even so, the sequence provides a useful indication of how wildlife activity has changed during the restoration period. Native forest provides birds with food and shelter, while the removal of invasive vegetation can help restore the variety of plants on which the wider ecosystem depends.Pest management has formed another part of the effort. Possums, rats, hedgehogs and mice can put pressure on native wildlife, so local groups have supported control work intended to reduce their impact. The Methven and Foothills Birdsong Initiative has been among the community organisations involved in efforts to improve conditions for native birds.Volunteers have helped sustain the restoration workStaveley Camp is used by community organisations, retreat groups and schools, giving the forest a role beyond conservation. Volunteer weeding days and environmental education activities have brought hundreds of people into contact with the site and helped build local involvement in its care.The work has also encouraged neighbouring landowners to pay closer attention to native bush on their own properties. Protecting forest remnants often depends on decisions made beyond a single reserve or campsite, particularly where invasive plants can spread from nearby land.De Spa's responsibilities expanded considerably from the initial weed-control contract. She sought funding, arranged volunteer sessions, supported school programmes and documented the history of Staveley Camp and its forest in a book. Her departure from the coordinator role is planned for the end of 2026, after nine years overseeing the project.Sycamores and cotoneaster remain among the plants requiring attention, and continued funding will be needed to prevent cleared areas from becoming overrun again.Biological control adds another toolThe restoration effort has also included biological control of an invasive plant known as Chilean flame creeper. Earlier in 2026, the team released Chilean flame creeper beetles, which are used to help control the plant.The approach differs from manually removing unwanted trees and shrubs. Biological control uses a selected organism to suppress an invasive species, potentially reducing the need for repeated intervention. Its effectiveness depends on how the control agent establishes and affects the target plant, so it is part of a longer management process rather than an immediate solution.At Staveley Camp, this work sits alongside the continued removal of invasive plants and the control of introduced mammals. The combination reflects the range of pressures affecting native forest remnants and the different methods needed to address them.Protecting existing forest can deliver lasting gainsEnvironment Canterbury biodiversity advisor Tilly King said, “Staveley Camp is a great example of what can be achieved when communities, landowners and councils work together over many years,” she said.The five-year monitoring period has recorded native regeneration and increased birdlife, while the longer restoration effort has helped the forest recover from years of invasive plant growth.

articles.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
articles.summary: The tech billionaire accuses Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using the network for military activity.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.

Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".

Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.

The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.

"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."

He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."

Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.

Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.

While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war .

Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.

Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.

The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.

Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

Fighting and aerial attacks continue to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.

Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.

Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.

It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.

Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.

articles.title: As Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin get ready to build a Moon base, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman gives an important update on Artemis IV, says: This agency knows very well …
articles.summary: NASA administrator Jared Isaacman recently shared an update on the launch of Artemis III stating that the agency is on track for docking exercises with
articles.body: NASA administrator Jared Isaacman recently shared an update on the launch of Artemis III stating that the agency is on track for docking exercises with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin lunar lander next year. “It’s about our own history. It’s a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months,” he said during a news conference at Kennedy Space Center. Isaacman said the “new space race” to land astronauts on the moon will be “much closer than it ever needed to be” because of slow going in past years.Isaacman’s update came six months after the successful Artemis II flight around the moon by four astronauts. According to a Fortune report, the agency plans to keep options open as long as possible before choosing between SpaceX and Blue Origin for the Artemis IV lunar lander that is scheduled for 2028.Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin get ready to build a Moon baseNASA plans to launch moon base near the moon’s south pole — nowhere near Apollo’s more equatorial locales. Both agencies – Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will launch their landers next year for docking practice by the three NASA astronauts and one Italian who will blast into orbit aboard NASA’s Orion capsule. The mission will be completed with three launches in quick succession from Cape Canaveral. Orion will dock first with Blue Origin’s Blue Ghost about 270 miles (435 kilometers) above Earth, before docking with SpaceX’s Starship at a slightly lower altitude.“As a rocket nerd, it’s going to be pretty awesome,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA’s associate administrator.“It is incredibly ambitious,” Rubio told The Associated Press earlier this month. “One thing I’ve always believed and learned is don’t bet against America.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: New Pentagon UFO files detail FBI agents' sighting of silent triangular object with no visible engines
articles.summary: FBI agents described a silent black triangular UAP hovering before accelerating at fighter-jet speeds in newly released Department of War documents.
articles.body: FBI agents reported witnessing a mysterious black triangular object hovering silently above a mountain ridge before suddenly accelerating at speeds comparable to a fighter jet, newly released Department of War documents reveal. The 2026 sighting is among several incidents detailed in the newly released records examining unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), alongside decades-old military encounters and reports of mysterious creatures, unexplained lights and supposed portals at a Utah ranch. One report from the FBI describes an encounter with a dark, nonreflective triangular object resembling a drone, with an estimated wingspan of 9 to 15 feet and no visible exhaust or conventional propulsion system. NEW TRUMP UFO FILE DUMP INCLUDES MILITARY FOOTAGE OF MYSTERIOUS STAR-SHAPED OBJECT The agents reported seeing the object rise vertically above a ridgeline before accelerating into a canyon without making a sound. A separate report from the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), which investigates reports of unidentified anomalous phenomena, provides a more detailed account of the encounter. VIDEO SHOWS US MILITARY TRACKING WHAT APPEARS TO BE MYSTERIOUS OBJECT FLYING OVER MIDDLE EAST IN 2025 The report describes a matte-black triangular object that climbed about 200 to 300 feet above a ridgeline, hovered for roughly 20 seconds and then appeared to accelerate almost instantly, disappearing into a canyon within two to three seconds. The witnesses described an object with no visible engines, rotors, exhaust or other conventional aircraft features. PENTAGON’S NEW UFO FILE RELEASE LOGS NEAR-MISS AS ‘SUPER-HEATED’ ORBS APPROACH US HELICOPTER Read the report here: The agents also reported observing a uniform heat signature across the object's surface through handheld thermal equipment, without the concentrated hot spots typically associated with propulsion systems. The Pentagon report notes that the object's speed was estimated by witnesses rather than measured by instruments. EX-PENTAGON OFFICIAL SAYS UAP FILES REVEAL 'TREASURE TROVE' OF INTELLIGENCE DATING BACK TO THE 1940S The two reports differ on the length of the encounter. The FBI described a sighting lasting approximately three seconds, while AARO detailed about 10 seconds of vertical ascent, 20 seconds of hovering and another two to three seconds of rapid flight before the object disappeared. Neither report identifies the object or establishes its origin. NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS Fox News Digital has contacted AARO for comment on the sighting, including whether the object has since been identified and whether images released with the FBI report show the actual encounter or are illustrations. The newly released records also include an Air Force intelligence report dated Jan. 19, 1957, detailing an unidentified radar contact involving a U.S. B-52 bomber during a Strategic Air Command mission near Saudi Arabia. PENTAGON DECLASSIFIES APOLLO 12 AUDIO OF ASTRONAUTS DESCRIBING UNEXPLAINED 'STREAKS OF LIGHT' IN SPACE The bomber was flying at about 39,000 feet when its radar detected an unidentified target roughly 6,000 yards away on Jan. 18, 1957. The contact remained on the aircraft's radar screen for five to seven minutes before disappearing as the bomber turned left. Air Force investigators noted that no other aircraft were expected in the area but acknowledged that the radar contact may have disappeared because of the bomber's change in direction. Other historical records describe reported sightings near California's Santa Catalina Island. In one case, three Boy Scouts attending summer camp reported seeing a silent, silver object moving faster than a conventional jet while hiking on the island June 25, 1952. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X The scouts claimed the object made a climbing turn before appearing to disintegrate, an Air Force intelligence report states. Investigators noted that the scouts had no instruments to measure its speed or altitude and that their limited experience made it difficult to assess the reliability of their account. Read the Catalina Island report here: A separate March 15, 1955, report describes a witness near Avalon on Catalina Island who spotted a bright, round object that changed from orange to red before falling straight down. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS The Air Force ultimately classified the sighting as a "probable meteor." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB The files also include a 60-page investigation conducted in 2010 by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) at a Utah ranch associated with reports of unexplained phenomena. SEND US A TIP Investigators interviewed residents who described towering dog-like creatures walking on two legs, mysterious balls of light and other unusual sightings. GOT A TIP? Other witnesses reported smaller, hairy creatures, a prehistoric-looking bird and a worm allegedly measuring 8 feet long. One witness also described a transparent, rippling structure she believed was a portal to another world. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST The investigation included eyewitness sketches, surveillance cameras, environmental monitoring and hair samples collected from areas associated with reported creature sightings. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Laboratory testing, however, identified the hair samples as coming from ordinary animals, including domestic dogs and a raccoon. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The report did not establish the existence of the alleged creatures or other extraordinary phenomena. Fox News Digital reached out to the FBI for comment.

articles.title: In the 1940s, Ohio built a 200-foot dam to supply water to a village; more than 80 years later, crews have begun removing it to restore a 14-mile creek and reconnect habitat across its tributary network
articles.summary: For over 80 years, a concrete dam in Ohio did what it was built for: supplied water to a village.
articles.body: For over 80 years, a concrete dam in Ohio did what it was built for: supplied water to a village. Now, the aging structure is being removed as part of a major restoration project. The aim of the project is bringing a creek back to its natural flow and improving water quality. It also wants to reconnect aquatic habitats that have been separated for decades now. The project was launched in October 2026 and it focuses on Cloverlick Creek in Clermont County, where officials hope removing the old structure will serve wildlife and people who fish, kayak and paddle in the region.The Cloverlick Dam is 200-foot-long and stands about 12 feet tall. It was built in the 1940s to provide water to the Village of Bethel. However, it has become an old structure and has now outlived its purpose. Bethel stopped operating its water treatment plant along the creek in 2006, leaving the dam redundant.Ohio to remove an 80-year-old damThe removal of the Cloverlick Dam is part of Ohio's H2Ohio initiative. It is a statewide programme focused on improving water quality and protecting natural resources. The Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR) broke ground on the project in October 2026. It worked with local conservation organisations, county agencies, the US Army Corps of Engineers and the Village of Bethel.Cloverlick Creek is approximately 14 miles and flows westward from Brown County into Clermont County. It is also part of a larger watershed, with around 70 miles of tributaries that officials want to reconnect through the restoration effort. The creek eventually feeds into William H. Harsha Lake, an important drinking-water source for the region.The problem with the old damIt’s not just the age that’s the problem. The dam has interrupted the natural flow of water which has created harmful conditions to aquatic life. Water becomes trapped behind the barrier and a pool is created where sediment and nutrients can accumulate. The slower-moving water can also become warmer, while oxygen levels may fall during the summer months.These changes affect the ecosystem. Fish have difficulty travelling. Sediment buildup can also damage the streambed and reduced oxygen can make conditions less suitable for aquatic organisms.As per the Clermont Soil and Water Conservation District, Cloverlick Creek has been classified as an impaired stream because its fish community has declined.A 14-mile creek and 70 miles of tributaries to reconnectOne of the most significant aims of the project is to restore connectivity across the creek. Rivers and streams function as connected systems, allowing fish and other aquatic organisms to move between habitats in search of food, shelter and breeding. A dam can interrupt these natural movements. In Cloverlick Creek, the concrete barrier has prevented fish migrating from Harsha Lake. Officials expect fish and other aquatic life to have a better condition after the structure is removed. The broader aim is to restore the creek's natural flow and reconnecting waterways can help improve habitat quality.Why removing the dam could improve water qualityRemoving the barrier will allow Cloverlick Creek to return towards a more natural flow pattern. However, restoration does not mean that every environmental problem will disappear immediately. The creek will need time to adjust. According to WVXU's report, ODNR programme manager Jon Horn said fish, aquatic insects and other indicators of water quality can respond within a year of dam removal.Safety risk for swimmersCloverlick Dam has also been identified as a public safety hazard. Low-head dams are sometimes called drowning machines because water flowing over their relatively low barriers can create powerful recirculating currents downstream which can trap swimmers sometimes. Removing it is expected to make the creek safer for activities such as paddling, kayaking and fishing.Funding the restorationAccording to ODNR, the H2Ohio Rivers Program is contributing $920,000, while the department's Division of Wildlife received an additional $1.1 million through the federal America the Beautiful Challenge grant programme.The project is expected to be substantially complete by fall 2027, according to the local conservation district.A dam built eight decades ago today is redundant and being demolished. In Cloverlick Creek, the aim is to replace it with a healthier and more connected stream system.

articles.title: Millions of people high blood pressure pills daily, now scientists are testing a small device that stimulates nerves through ear, and a trial found it safe and easy to use at home
articles.summary: The worst thing about blood pressure medication is that they are for life. Once a person has been put on BP medication, it is for life in most cases.
articles.body: The worst thing about blood pressure medication is that they are for life. Once a person has been put on BP medication, it is for life in most cases. Doctors might adjust dosage but weaning from this medicine is quite uncommon. However a promising research published in the American Heart Association shows that blood pressure can actually be brought down by stimulating the ear with a small device.This tiny device is said to deliver gentle electrical pulses through the ear. This can be a brand new approach to treating difficult high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.The device did not significantly reduce blood pressure across the entire group compared with a placebo. However, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising responses. The researchers believe that stimulating nerves in the ear could one day offer another treatment option for people who continue to struggle with high blood pressure despite taking medication.The findings are from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. While the initial results are promising for some patients, researchers say further studies involving larger groups are necessary to establish how effective the treatment is and identify those most likely to benefit.How stimulating nerves in the ear may help control blood pressureThe treatment, known as transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), is designed to influence the autonomic nervous system. This system regulates several functions that happen automatically in the body, including heartbeat, digestion and blood pressure.The researchers are investigating whether mild electrical stimulation delivered through the ear can help the body regulate blood pressure more effectively. Unlike procedures that require surgery or instruments to be placed inside the body, this technique is non-invasive.The device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, is handheld and fitted with two small clips that attach to the tragus, the cartilage flap just outside the ear canal. The clips deliver low-level electrical pulses to the nerves in the area. Patients can operate the device themselves, making it possible to use the treatment at home.Trial involving 63 patients examines safety and effectivenessFunded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), the trial included 63 people whose blood pressure remained above target levels despite taking at least one blood pressure-lowering medication.Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group received active electrical stimulation, while the other used a sham device that served as a control. Comparing the two groups allowed researchers to examine whether the treatment itself made a difference to blood pressure.During the first two weeks, participants were asked to use their assigned devices for 30 minutes every day. For the next 10 weeks, they continued treatment once a week.The device was found to be safe and generally well tolerated during the study. Most participants also adhered to the prescribed schedule, indicating that the treatment may be manageable for people using it as part of their routine at home.However, safety and ease of use do not necessarily mean that the treatment is effective at lowering blood pressure. Further research will be needed to establish its benefits, particularly for people whose hypertension remains difficult to control with medication.Hope for people with uncontrolled BPEven though no significant overall benefit could be witnessed in this limited human trial, scientists have found an important finding in patients with very high BP.As reported by Science Daily, Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham."As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."This suggests the technique could be especially helpful for people whose blood pressure is hardest to control. But the trial was small, and these subgroup results will need to be confirmed in larger studies before anyone can say how well it really works.

articles.title: An Australian wildlife conservancy bought 200 hectares on King Island to protect threatened species; one native bird it hopes to save has fewer than 100 individuals remaining
articles.summary: The Australian Wildlife Conservancy (AWC) has purchased 200 hectares of land on King Island, Tasmania, to protect threatened wildlife, including a
articles.body: The Australian Wildlife Conservancy (AWC) has purchased 200 hectares of land on King Island, Tasmania, to protect threatened wildlife, including a critically endangered bird with fewer than 100 individuals remaining. The acquisition marks the organisation’s first conservation project in Tasmania and creates an opportunity to expand efforts to protect the island’s unique species.According to the Australian Wildlife Conservancy, the property, named Boulder Wildlife Sanctuary, lies beside Lavinia State Reserve on King Island’s north-east coast. The property contains native vegetation that provides important habitat for threatened species. AWC plans to work with the local community to protect remaining habitats and address threats from feral cats, invasive weeds and fire.AWC buys 200 hectares on King Island to protect rare wildlifeThe acquisition of Boulder Wildlife Sanctuary marked AWC’s first expansion into Tasmania. The 200-hectare property at 87 Martha Lavinia Road, on King Island, offered an opportunity to build on conservation work already undertaken by residents and organisations. AWC lays the foundation for a King Island Conservation Program to be developed.The property lies alongside Lavinia State Reserve on the island’s north-east coast and supports threatened and high conservation value native vegetation. AWC Chief Executive Tim Allard said, “Locals have worked for decades to protect the island’s unique natural heritage.”“This acquisition represents an opportunity for AWC to build on the strong conservation foundations already established on the island and deliver our conservation model where it can have the greatest impact.”King Island’s 70% native vegetation loss threatens its unique wildlifeKing Island lies in Bass Strait, between Victoria and Tasmania, and is recognised internationally as a Key Biodiversity Area. It supports 470 native plant species, 164 bird species, 12 mammal species and nine reptile species. Among its birds are seven threatened and two critically endangered endemic subspecies. However, the island has experienced substantial environmental decline since European settlement, with 70% of its native vegetation cleared for agriculture. The remaining habitats have become highly fragmented, contributing to the local loss of several species, including the Forty-spotted Pardalote, Glossy Black-Cockatoo and Gang-gang Cockatoo.A bird with fewer than 100 individuals faces a fight for survivalThe critically endangered King Island Scrubtit is among the subspecies AWC hopes to protect at Boulder Wildlife Sanctuary. Its population has declined to fewer than 100 individuals, spread across three known isolated subpopulations. The bird is rarer by population estimate than the California Condor, with 500 individuals, New Zealand’s Kakapo, with 250, and the Whooping Crane, with 600.As an endemic bird, the King Island Scrubtit depends on mature, dense wet forests, particularly swamp paperbark (Melaleuca ericifolia) forest. Much of this habitat has been cleared for agriculture or degraded by altered fire regimes. The subspecies is a priority for conservation under the Australian Government’s Threatened Species Action Plan.AWC targets feral cats and weeds to protect King Island’s rare wildlifeAWC plans to begin with a comprehensive ecological survey to establish a scientific baseline for wildlife at Boulder Wildlife Sanctuary. Initial work will include feral animal and weed control, fire management planning and habitat restoration to improve connectivity where possible. The organisation intends to expand its efforts beyond the property to address threats across King Island, particularly feral cat populations.The conservation work comes as wildlife on the island faces an ongoing H5 bird flu outbreak, which has taken a substantial toll on coastal birds and marine mammals in Bass Strait. AWC hopes long-term, science-based conservation and collaboration with local groups will help stabilise and ultimately recover the King Island Scrubtit population while protecting other threatened species.
